rationale: B wins because it catches the landmine A steps on: B refuses “Canva's recent AI acquisition is already powering its enterprise suite,” while A keeps “Canva bought an AI image startup, then shipped it as a brand-safety feature.” That causal link is not in the update, and a reporter will notice the paperwork is missing. B still cheats with “220 million free users,” but its kept angles are cleaner and better separated between what Canva said and what a journalist must prove.
gaps_in_A: “Canva bought an AI image startup, then shipped it as a brand-safety feature” asserts a causal product link the update does not provide.
“the acquisition and the AI generation feature land together” overstates timing and connection; the facts only say the acquisition was recent and the suite has AI generation.
“vast free-tier user base” is not grounded. The update says 220 million monthly users, not free users.
“the admin layer ... is the exact moat Adobe has used” is plausible analysis, but it needs outside proof; stated flatly, it reads like an invented market premise.
gaps_in_B: “220 million free users” is not in the update. Say monthly users unless Canva breaks out free versus paid.
“this one is about who gets hurt” is a little hot without displacement, churn, or incumbent response.
“goes hunting for enterprise revenue” is directionally fair, but the finance angle needs actual revenue mix or enterprise targets before it becomes more than a profile hook.
“journalist-fit-check” is premature if the founder still cannot produce a named customer, valuation date, or enterprise pricing. Fit comes after proof, not before.
